title: SLU, UTD Fight For First Place As Collegiate Chess League Heads To Playoffs
summary:
Saint Louis University (SLU) and the University of Texas, Dallas (UTD) are locked in a tight race for first place in the Collegiate Chess League as teams approach the end of the regular season and push for playoff seeding. With most teams having just two matches remaining, SLU, with a 4.5/5 score, has the inside track to the top seed, while UTD has the most total points with 5/6. The Quarterfinals take place on November 14.

Division I Standings: Fall 2026

Mizzou Catches SLU In Dramatic Final Round

SLU and the University of Missouri, Columbia (Mizzou) have been the most dominant teams in the Collegiate Chess League for most of the last few years. This season, SLU has thrived, competing for the top seed while Mizzou has struggled, losing matches to UTD and Texas Tech. Despite their different fortunes, the match between these teams was the most competitive of any in division one this season.

SLU started well, winning the first round 3-1 and the second 2.5-1.5. A 2-2 third round meant that SLU needed just one point out of the four final-round games to take the match. However, Mizzou saved their best for last, dominating the final round 3.5-0.5, and earning an 8-8 tie, the only tied match of the season so far.

Here's a clutch victory by GM Aryan Tari in the final round that helped to secure the match tie.

SLU Defeats Defending Champion UTD

The last-round collapse against Mizzou has been the only blemish on SLU's otherwise stellar season. Their most impressive victory came against the defending champions from UTD, a team that has won their other five matches. UTD held a narrow 4.5-3.5 edge after two rounds, but SLU dominated the second half of the match, taking seven of eight points. That success earned them a comfortable final margin of 10.5-5.5.

GM Viktor Gazik led the way for SLU, scoring 3.5/5, including the following victory against GM Sankalp Gupta.

Check out the week six broadcast by Joe Lee.

The Collegiate Chess League is the premier online chess competition for college students.

title: FIDE appoints Emil Sutovsky CEO of FIDE Enterprises
summary: The International Chess Federation (FIDE) has appointed Grandmaster Emil Sutovsky as CEO of FIDE Enterprises, a Swiss-based company wholly owned by FIDE. He will combine this role with his current position as Chief Executive Adviser to FIDE President Timur Turlov. In his new role, Sutovsky will oversee FIDE’s commercial activities, with an emphasis on building long-term partnerships and developing new business opportunities. The appointment forms part of FIDE’s broader efforts to strengthen its institutional and commercial capabilities. FIDE Enterprises will support the Federation’s long-term development by helping to unlock the commercial potential of chess. Another priority will be to strengthen the connection between professional chess and its global audience, making the sport more engaging and accessible to a wider public.

title: FIDE strengthens its presidential representation and advisory team
summary: FIDE is expanding its system of presidential representatives and advisers as part of the organisational changes announced on 26 October 2026. Together with the previously announced representatives, the new members will contribute to strengthening the political and institutional role of the President’s team within FIDE. They will support the Federation’s international interests and maintain direct dialogue with the global chess community. Three professionals will take on new roles. Håkan Jalling – Representative of the President for Olympic Games Inclusion Håkan Jalling, President of the Nordic Chess Federation and former President of the Swedish Chess Federation, has been closely involved in efforts to strengthen chess’s position within the Olympic movement. Under his leadership, the Swedish Chess Federation gained recognition from the Swedish Olympic Committee in April 2026. He also chairs the European Chess Union’s Chess Olympic Affairs Commission. Jalling will contribute to FIDE’s efforts to promote the inclusion of chess in the Olympic Games programme, drawing on Sweden’s experience. His work will include supporting relations between national chess federations and their national Olympic committees, in cooperation with other members of the FIDE team involved in this area. Darcy Lima – Representative of the President for Institutional Dialogue Brazilian Grandmaster Darcy Lima is a former President of the Brazilian Chess Federation with many years of experience in international chess. Lima will contribute to FIDE’s efforts to strengthen institutional dialogue within the global chess community. His work will include facilitating cooperation between federations and encouraging the exchange of experience and best practices, in coordination with other members of the FIDE team working in related areas. Alexander Martynov – Senior Advisor to the President Alexander Martynov will provide advice to the FIDE President on strategic and organisational matters. His responsibilities will include supporting the President’s priority initiatives and contributing to the development of the federation’s long-term agenda. The system of presidential representatives is being developed as an important channel for political dialogue and institutional cooperation within FIDE. Working alongside previously announced representatives, Jalling and Lima will help strengthen the Federation’s engagement with chess organisations and the international sports movement. Martynov’s appointment will further reinforce the advisory support available to the President.

title: World Senior Championships underway in Serbia: Cramling, Georgiev and Gaprindashvili among participants
summary:
Four tournaments across two age groups

The 2026 FIDE World Senior Chess Championships are taking place in Vrnjačka Banja, Serbia, from 3 to 14 November. A total of 385 players representing 65 national federations have gathered at the Hotel Zepter, with four world titles up for grabs. The field includes 44 grandmasters and eight women's grandmasters.

The championships are divided into two age groups, 50+ and 65+, each featuring an open and a women's section. All four tournaments follow an 11-round Swiss system, with a time control of 90 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by an additional 30 minutes, and a 30-second increment from move one.

The first round was played on Tuesday 3 November, and the competition will continue with one round per day until Saturday 14 November, except for a rest day on Sunday 8 November. Games begin at 15.00 local time, with the final round starting an hour earlier. The total prize fund amounts to €50,000, including special prizes for players aged 75 and over.

Among the participants are several familiar names from international chess, including Pia Cramling from Sweden, Kiril Georgiev from Bulgaria, Zurab Sturua from Georgia and former women's world champion Nona Gaprindashvili, also from Georgia.

title: Peter Leko and Peter Svidler to commentate on the Gukesh v. Sindarov Geneva match
summary:
Peter Leko and Peter Svidler will provide the official commentary for the 2026 FIDE World Championship match between Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva. Leko brings first-hand experience of playing for the world title, while Svidler combines extensive top-level experience with a long-standing reputation as a commentator. Their coverage will accompany the 14-game match, which begins on 24 November at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny. | Image: FIDE

The two Peters

If you are going to watch a World Championship, you want the best voices in your ears. FIDE has given us two of them.

On 2 November 2026, FIDE announced on X that GMs Peter Leko and Peter Svidler will be the commentators for the Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026, where Gukesh Dommaraju will defend his title against Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva. The first game is scheduled to take place on 24 November.

Peter Leko knows what it feels like to sit at that board. In 2004, he played Vladimir Kramnik for the world title in Brissago, the last time Switzerland hosted a World Championship match. Since then, he has become one of the most loved commentators in chess. He is warm, he is honest, and he explains a position so that even a club player can follow it.

Peter Svidler has won the Russian Championship eight times, the first at the age of 18 in 1994. His mix of deep knowledge and dry humour makes even a quiet draw worth watching.

Peter Leko is also a huge chess fan himself | Photo: Charlotte Chess Center

Peter Svidler is an eight-time Russian champion and one of the most appreciated commentators in chess | Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE

The World Championship match is played to the best of 14 classical games, and many of the games are long, slow and full of ideas you can't see at first. Good commentators turn a quiet position into a lesson. With two top grandmasters at the desk, we will get Gukesh's and Sindarov's thinking explained move by move.

The match will be played at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, Geneva, and tickets are already on sale. Mark your calendars. See you in Geneva!

title: Suleymenov on Gukesh, Sindarov and the psychological side of chess
summary:
Chennai has given GM Alisher Suleymenov a title and a reason to return. After winning the 1st Chola Chess International GM Round Robin earlier this year, the Kazakh grandmaster is back for the 1st Chola Chess GM 2026. In this interview with Devansh Singh, he recalls beating a 12-year-old Gukesh Dommaraju and explains why he considers Javokhir Sindarov the favourite in the World Championship match. He also speaks about his ambitions in chess and the importance of staying psychologically strong. | Photo: ChessBase India

Interview with Alisher Suleymenov

GM Alisher Suleymenov of Kazakhstan is back in Chennai, the city where he won the 1 st Chola Chess International GM Round Robin earlier this year. He is the 21 st seed at the Chola GM Open. Devansh Singh from the ChessBase India team spoke with him about why Chennai keeps drawing him back, the day he beat a 12-year-old Gukesh Dommaraju, the upcoming World Championship match and the psychological aspects of chess.

Devansh: Welcome to Chennai again, Alisher. Last time you played here, it was the 1st Chola Chess GM Round Robin, and you won that event. This is the first time a tournament of this strength is happening in India with average rating 2412 and 30–35 grandmasters. How does it feel to play this kind of event in India?

Alisher: It's wonderful. I want to thank Chola Chess again for inviting me. I really enjoy playing in Chennai, and in India overall. I believe this is my seventh time in India, and the third time in Chennai, because I also played the 44 th Chess Olympiad here. I pretty much have only good memories of Chennai - I played very well at the Olympiad and gained even more rating points there than in the Round Robin event. And I always enjoy the conditions that the All India Chess Federation and Chola Chess provide. I have visited over 30 countries. During the 44 th FIDE Chess Olympiad, the hotel we stayed in was the best. Also, everything here is just perfect.

Devansh: In that Round Robin tournament, you were the invited grandmaster while the Indian international masters were chasing norms, and some of them are grandmasters now. When you play such an event, do you feel extra motivation, knowing they have to get past you? Some players just play for draws in these events. You are not one of them.

Alisher: I was very happy when I got invited, because the average rating of the tournament was almost like mine - a very strong event. And I want to say that the idea of Chola Chess, inviting specifically young foreigners, is a very good idea. In most Round Robin events around the world, organisers invite older grandmasters who have sort of quit chess - they are not motivated, they don't work on chess - and it is much easier to earn a GM norm there. This time it was tough, because almost all the foreigners were young, motivated, hardworking professionals. The long-term growth is much more important than short-term achievements. After that tournament, I went straight to an open tournament in Russia and won it despite not being the favourite - so Chola was good training as well.

Devansh: Let's come to this tournament. Today you played one of the most talented girls in Indian chess, Shubhi. How was the game?

Alisher: A very equal game, I believe. In the opening, I was slightly better, with long-term pressure and no risk. From one point, she started defending very well. I won a pawn, but she got very active pieces in the endgame, and at once I missed a defensive resource of hers, after which it was just a draw. Before that, I could have tried something better - I would probably have posed more practical problems - but objectively it was still very much a draw.

Alisher Suleymenov at the board during the Chola GM Open 2026

Devansh: The World Championship match is coming up. You have played both Gukesh and Sindarov in classical chess. Who do you think has the upper hand?

Alisher: I played once against Gukesh, when he was 2500, and I was 2430 - I was 19, he was 12. That was in Russia, at the Aeroflot Open 2019. Usually, there is one round a day, but because of some issues on the first day, they had to make a double round, and we played in the afternoon. He was quite small and might have been tired. I played extremely well, and even now I am proud of that game. Then we played at the World Rapid Championship in Samarkand 2023 - I was sort of winning there too, but the position remained complicated. I couldn't maintain my advantage, and Gukesh managed to outcalculate me very well.

Against Sindarov, I have played much more in classical chess, and honestly, looking at the positions we got, I should have had a plus score against him - but I kept losing completely winning or just dead-drawn positions. I was not able to make even a single draw against him. Once I was completely winning; another time I had more time and a nearly decisive advantage. So from my own experience of facing both of them, psychologically I believe Sindarov is a bit stronger, and that is the main reason I consider him the favourite. But I don't want to say I am rooting for anybody - I just want to see a very good match between two very strong players. Sindarov was never happy to just make a draw from a losing position against me; in drawn positions he was always trying to beat me, and to beat anyone, given the chance. He is a real fighter, I believe.

Gukesh Dommaraju | Photo: Nils Rohde

Devansh: You have played almost all the top players - Carlsen, Praggnanandhaa, Sindarov, Gukesh.

Alisher: Gukesh, Sindarov, Pragg, Abdusattorov I have played them - not all of them, but most of them.

Devansh: You are seeded 21 st here by rating. What is your target? To win the tournament, or just to play well?

Alisher: For everybody, when you go to a tournament, you should always aim for the best. The ambitious aim would be to win the tournament, but I understand it is extremely strong, so I just want to play well and see how it goes.

Devansh: Doesn't aiming to win put extra pressure on you during the games or in preparation?

Alisher: You have such great questions. I have a 17-year career already. When you are less experienced and play close to ten tournaments a year, always aiming for the best, it creates extra expectations, and it backfired for me many times. With experience, you understand that these days everybody plays chess very well - you respect your opponents but still try for the best. I am happy that I managed to have no stress despite high aims. This year, apart from Chola Chess, I won two international tournaments, and I went there with high aims as usual. The psychological part in chess is extremely important.

Devansh: Take an ambitious player around 2200-2300 going for their first title or norm. Ambition creates pressure, but just playing without it can kill motivation. How do you manage that balance?

Alisher: I believe it depends a lot on concentration, and you should have a balance of both attitudes, because each can have drawbacks. It usually comes with experience. But if you have to pick one, and you are not experienced enough yet, I would still go with ambition - long-term, it is much better. I can compare two youngsters I have in mind - I won't say who. One is chess-wise just better, the other is psychologically better. Recently, I saw that the first one performed worse because he was not psychologically ready, while the other guy thinks he is super strong - and that really helps him, although it wastes too much energy sometimes. It is very individual. And it is not enough to have very good chess understanding - you have to play well, and you cannot keep working on the same things in the same manner. You have to work on everything for long-term improvement.

Devansh: Thanks for your time, Alisher! It's been nice talking to you.

Alisher: Thank you so much!
